expectedText:
NON-DISCLOSURE AGREEMENT
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

WHAT COUNTS AS CONFIDENTIAL
This agreement can define Acme, Inc.'s confidential information broadly — the parties are free to agree on what counts. But if Acme, Inc. ever needs to enforce protection through trade secret law specifically, rather than just this contract, only information that actually meets the legal definition qualifies: information whose owner has taken reasonable measures to keep it secret, and that has independent economic value because it isn't generally known or easily discovered by others who could profit from it. Information that's already public, or that Jordan Lee already knew before this agreement, doesn't become a trade secret just because this agreement calls it confidential.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-29]
  "the term "trade secret" means all forms and types of financial, business, scientific, technical, economic, or engineering information ... if— (A) the owner thereof has taken reasonable measures to keep such information secret; and (B) the information derives independent economic value, actual or potential, from not being generally known to, and not being readily ascertainable through proper means by, another person who can obtain economic value from the disclosure or use of the information"
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1839(3) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, definition of "trade secret" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1839)
  "the definition of trade secret consists of three elements: (1) information, (2) that is valuable because it is unknown to others, and (3) that the owner has attempted to keep secret."
  — Inteliclear, LLC v. ETC Global Holdings, Inc., 978 F.3d 653 (9th Cir. 2020) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4796836/inteliclear-llc-v-etc-global-holdings/)
  "both Michalski and Kamik have a great deal of general skill and knowledge as engineers who have studied for and worked in this area for years. These skills are not specific to the techniques and processes used by Analog, and both engineers are free to market those skills to competitors."
  — Analog Devices, Inc. v. Michalski, 157 N.C. App. 462, 579 S.E.2d 449 (2003) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1304930/analog-devices-inc-v-michalski/)
  Known gap: This describes the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act's definition specifically. State trade secret law (most states have adopted a version of the Uniform Trade Secrets Act) uses a similar two-part test, but this clause was checked against the federal definition only, not each state's exact statutory wording. Separately, this definition doesn't override a well-established doctrine outside the statute's text: an employee's own general skill, knowledge, and experience — the things they'd know how to do regardless of which employer taught it to them — aren't the employer's trade secret just because the employee developed or sharpened them on this job, and courts have declined to read confidentiality agreements to stop someone from taking that general know-how to their next employer.

CONFIDENTIALITY OBLIGATIONS
Jordan Lee will keep Acme, Inc.'s confidential information private, use it only to do the work Acme, Inc. asked for, and take reasonable care to prevent anyone else from accessing it.

WHAT THIS AGREEMENT DOESN'T COVER
This agreement doesn't restrict information that was already public, that Jordan Lee already knew before receiving it from Acme, Inc., that Jordan Lee develops independently without using Acme, Inc.'s confidential information, or that Jordan Lee is required to disclose by law — though Jordan Lee will tell Acme, Inc. first if legally able to.

WHISTLEBLOWER IMMUNITY NOTICE
Federal law requires Acme, Inc. to give Jordan Lee this notice: Jordan Lee cannot be held criminally or civilly liable under federal or state trade secret law for disclosing a trade secret in confidence to a government official or an attorney, solely to report or investigate a suspected violation of law, or in a court filing made under seal. This notice is here because federal law requires it in any agreement governing the use of confidential information — an employer that omits it loses the right to certain enhanced damages and attorney's fees against this recipient in a future trade secret lawsuit, even one unrelated to whistleblowing.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-29]
  "An individual shall not be held criminally or civilly liable under any Federal or State trade secret law for the disclosure of a trade secret that— (A) is made— (i) in confidence to a Federal, State, or local government official, either directly or indirectly, or to an attorney; and (ii) solely for the purpose of reporting or investigating a suspected violation of law; or (B) is made in a complaint or other document filed in a lawsuit or other proceeding, if such filing is made under seal."
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1833(b)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, whistleblower immunity (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1833)
  "An employer shall provide notice of the immunity set forth in this subsection in any contract or agreement with an employee that governs the use of a trade secret or other confidential information. ... If an employer does not comply with the notice requirement in subparagraph (A), the employer may not be awarded exemplary damages or attorney fees under subparagraph (C) or (D) of section 1836(b)(3) in an action against an employee to whom notice was not provided."
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1833(b)(3) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, notice requirement and consequence (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1833)
  "An employer shall be considered to be in compliance with the notice requirement in subparagraph (A) if the employer provides a cross-reference to a policy document provided to the employee that sets forth the employer’s reporting policy for a suspected violation of law."
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1833(b)(3)(B) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, policy-document alternative to contract notice (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1833)
  "An individual who files a lawsuit for retaliation by an employer for reporting a suspected violation of law may disclose the trade secret to the attorney of the individual and use the trade secret information in the court proceeding, if the individual— (A) files any document containing the trade secret under seal; and (B) does not disclose the trade secret, except pursuant to court order."
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1833(b)(2) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, use of trade secret information in an anti-retaliation lawsuit (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1833)
  Known gap: The immunity itself only covers disclosures made to report or investigate a suspected legal violation, or made under seal in litigation — it doesn't protect using a trade secret for any other purpose, including ordinary competition after leaving the company. Two related points the notice above doesn't spell out: an employer can satisfy this same notice requirement without putting it in a contract at all, by cross-referencing a separate policy document that states the employer's reporting policy instead; and someone who is retaliated against for reporting a suspected violation has a further right beyond the immunity itself — they may share the trade secret with their own attorney and use it in that retaliation lawsuit, if the filing is made under seal. No case law addressing enforcement of this specific notice-and-consequence provision was found in this research; the statute's own text is unambiguous about the notice requirement and its consequence, so the statute stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to indicate your agreement to the terms above.

Recipient: Jordan Lee
Date: _______________

—
